attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, giving his view of what will burst the bubble.

semantics.note: 'I maintain that part of the collapse will be' is a firm, unhedged forecast. 'Most likely Microsoft or Google' only qualifies which firm is punished; the core commitment is a collapse that includes investor punishment. No deadline was given.

contract.note: Requiring both a recognisable collapse and documented punishment as part of it is faithful, because the statement assumes a collapse is coming. The 'long period' in the contradiction condition is vague, but it does not change the result here.

evidence.note: Microsoft fell about 10% in one day in Jan 2026 on worries about AI spending. That is investor punishment, but it was not part of any bubble collapse.
Indicates no collapse by Oct 2026, with demand still above supply. With no deadline, the absence of a collapse so far does not show the forecast failed.

reviews.rationale: This is a firm forecast with no deadline. Investors did punish Microsoft for AI spending (e1), but no recognised collapse of the AI bubble had happened by the evaluation date (e2), so the early-resolution rule is not met. Absence before an open-ended horizon is not failure, so the claim stays unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own summary judgement, written after paraphrasing Covello. The sentence is in his voice.

semantics.note: A compound present-tense observation. 'Path to boosting revenues is unclear' is a judgement and is rightly left unscored.

contract.note: 'Isn't making anybody any money' is an unqualified universal. Reading it to include sellers of genAI products and infrastructure is the ordinary reading, not a stretch. The H1 2024 window fits a statement made in July 2024.

evidence.note: Nvidia earned $14.9B net income for the quarter to Apr 2024. That is total company income; read with e2, it shows large money made from genAI demand.
The CEO attributes record data-centre growth to genAI training and inference demand. This is a company disclosure, which is the company-reported basis the contract asks for.
Microsoft reported 7 points of Azure growth from AI and 1.8M paid Copilot subscribers: company-reported genAI revenue in the target period. It does not measure jobs.
Covers AI-skill job postings broadly since 2012, not generative AI alone, so it does not settle the jobs part.

reviews.rationale: The contract treats the claim as false if any firm part is clearly false. Company-reported results from H1 2024 show substantial genAI-linked revenue and profit: Nvidia's data-centre surge credited to genAI, and Microsoft's Azure AI and paid Copilot revenue. That contradicts 'isn't making anybody any money'. The jobs part is not settled by e4, and the revenue-path part is a judgement.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: A present-tense claim about generative AI's efficiency trend. 'Much more' has no threshold.

contract.note: Resources per comparable-quality output is an ordinary technical reading, and the contract excludes price cuts, which protects the speaker. A cost-based reading is possible from context, so interpretation matters, but the chosen reading is not stretched.

evidence.note: The DeepSeek-V2 preprint (May 2024) reports better quality with about 93% less KV cache and 5.76x generation throughput on the same 8-GPU node. This is developer-reported but comes with stated hardware and workloads, as the contract allows.

reviews.rationale: Within the Apr–Jun 2024 window, a publicly released model showed large reductions in resources per comparable-or-better output on fixed hardware. That meets the contract's contradiction condition. The caveat is that this is a single developer-reported comparison, not an independent replication.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post's conclusion.

semantics.note: A present-tense claim about current apps and the visible pipeline. Reading 'on the horizon' as the state of the pipeline at publication is reasonable.

contract.note: The ordinary sense of 'killer app' (compelling value driving sustained adoption) is fair, but no threshold exists, so the result depends on that interpretation.

evidence.note: Company disclosure: 1.8M paid Copilot subscribers, growing 35% quarter on quarter, with claimed customer benefits. A serious candidate, but it does not show retention, active use or independently verified gains.
An independent six-country survey (Mar–Apr 2024) finds frequent ChatGPT use rare. This supports the claim for consumers only and cannot rule out a professional killer app.

reviews.rationale: The evidence points both ways and fits no threshold. Consumer use was mostly infrequent (e8), while coding assistance had large paid adoption by Microsoft's own report (e7), without evidence of retention or sustained use. The packet does not establish whether any application met the killer-app standard, and no forthcoming-product evidence was readable.
